title: ASCII
body:
**American Standard Code for Information Interchange**: the character encoding the 68000
and its toolchain assume. A 7-bit code, so 128 characters, stored one per [[Byte]] with the
top bit spare. That spare bit is what every "extended ASCII" scheme fought over before
Unicode settled it.

## The layout worth remembering

| Range (hex) | Decimal | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `$00`–`$1F` | 0–31 | control characters (`NUL`, `LF` = `$0A`, `CR` = `$0D`, `ESC` = `$1B`) |
| `$20` | 32 | space |
| `$30`–`$39` | 48–57 | digits `0`–`9` |
| `$41`–`$5A` | 65–90 | uppercase `A`–`Z` |
| `$61`–`$7A` | 97–122 | lowercase `a`–`z` |
| `$7F` | 127 | `DEL` |

Two consequences that show up in assignments:

- **Digit to value**: subtract `$30`. The character `'7'` is `$37`; `$37 - $30 = 7`. This is
  the whole of a naive `atoi`.
- **Case flip**: uppercase and lowercase differ by exactly `$20`, one bit. `or #$20` forces
  lowercase, `and #$DF` forces uppercase, `eor #$20` toggles. See [[Binary Operations]].

The ordering is also why `'A' < 'a'` in C and why a naive sort puts `Zebra` before `apple`.

## In this course

[[Character Representation]] means ASCII here. A string is a run of bytes; C terminates it
with a `$00`, which is why `NUL` is character zero rather than something useful. The
[[6850 ACIA]] hands you an ASCII byte per keypress, and the terminal turns bytes back into
glyphs, so the encoding is the contract at both ends of [[I-O]].
